corrected_text: The religion of the ancient Cappadocians was much the same with that of the Persians. At Comana there was a rich and stately temple dedicated to Bellona; whose battles the priests and their attendants used to repeat on stated days, cutting and wounding each other as if fired with an enthusiastic fury. No less famous and magnificent were the temples of Apollo Cataenius, and of Jupiter: the last of which had 3000 fixed servants, or religious votaries. The chief priest was next in rank to that of Comana; and, according to Strabo, had an yearly revenue of 15 talents. Diana Perica was worshipped in a city called Capadocia, where women, devoted to the worship of that goddess, were reported to tread barefooted on burning coals, without receiving any hurt. The temples of Diana at Diopolis, and of Annis at Zela, were likewise held in great veneration both by the Cappadocians and Armenians, who flocked to them from all parts. In the latter were tended all oaths in matters of consequence; and the chief among the priests was no way inferior in dignity, power, and wealth, to any in the kingdom; having a royal attendance, and an unlimited authority over all the inferior servants and officers of the temple. The Romans, who willingly adopted all the superstitions and superstitious rites of the nations they conquered, greatly increased the revenues of this and other temples; conferring the priesthood on such as they thought most fit for carrying on their designs. We are told that human sacrifices were offered at Comana; and that this barbarous custom was brought by Orestes and his sister Iphigenia from Taurica Scythica, where men and women were immolated to Diana.
